vignette: He sits on the edge of the worn leather chair, knees pressed together, hands clasped so tightly the knuckles have gone white. The morning light cuts across the office floor, catching dust motes that dance like static in his peripheral vision. He does not look at the window. He never does anymore. Six years ago, he was walking home from a late shift at the county mental health clinic, a leather satchel full of intake forms heavy against his shoulder. The alley behind the old textile building was supposed to be a shortcut. A hand on his arm. A voice from the shadows. The smell of stale beer and damp concrete. He describes it now in a flat, even tone, as if reading a case file, but his breath hitches on the word resisted. He stopped fighting when the blade pressed against his ribs. He stopped moving when the violation took hold. He walked home two hours later, showered until his skin burned, and told his wife he had gotten locked out of the building. At fifty-three, he has spent the better part of his adult life working as a clinical social worker. Now, the work feels like wearing a uniform that no longer fits. His caseload quietly shrank. He began leaving his office door closed, a boundary his director praised as professional maturity. Inside, he feels like a fraud. His job was to sit with people in their worst moments, to offer a steady presence in the dark. Now, when a client in his office shifts forward, his heart hammers against his sternum. He catches himself flinching when a male colleague adjusts his jacket. He tells himself it is just burnout, just the weight of a field that asks too much of men who are taught to hold the line without buckling. At home, the distance between him and his wife has become a third presence in the bedroom. He loves her. He knows this in the way he remembers how she takes her coffee, how she hums while folding laundry, how her hand finds his shoulder when he sleeps. But touch now feels like a question he is afraid to answer. He wakes at 3 a.m., jaw clenched, replaying the angle of the streetlight, the scuff of a boot, the sound of his own breath catching in his throat. He rolls to the other side of the bed so his back faces her, telling himself he is just cold. He has learned the names of the symptoms, read the books about nervous systems and trauma loops, and takes notes on grounding techniques. He understands the theory. It does not stop the way his hands tremble when the office door clicks shut behind him. It does not stop him from scanning every room for exits before he sits down. In the present moment, he watches the clinician's pen move across a notepad. The scratch of the nib sounds too loud. He wonders if the words being written are about his recovery, or his failure, or something he cannot name but feels in his chest like a stone sinking through water. He exhales, slow and measured, the way he was taught to regulate his clients. The habit feels borrowed now. He leans forward, resting his elbows on his knees, and says he is tired of carrying it alone. The room stays quiet. He waits.
